n: About 23 years after Nebuchadnezzar’s death, Belshazzar throws a lavish feast for a thousand nobles. Historical records show he ruled Babylon as co-regent while his father Nabonidus was away; the Persian army was already near the city.

f.g: Son of Nabonidus, Babylon’s last king; he governed Babylon as co-regent around 550–539 BC.

n: Under the influence of wine, Belshazzar orders the sacred vessels from Jerusalem’s temple brought out for drinking. “Father” can mean ancestor or royal predecessor.

f.g: “Father” in ancient usage could mean predecessor or forebear.

n: The holy vessels used to worship God become party cups. This is deliberate sacrilege—mocking the God of Israel.
While drinking from God’s vessels, they praise idols of every material. The list echoes the metals of Nebuchadnezzar’s statue in chapter 2.

f.w: praised the gods of gold, and of silver

n: Suddenly the fingers of a human hand appear and write on the plaster wall near the lampstand, where the light is brightest. Archaeologists have found Babylon’s palace walls coated in white plaster.
The king turns pale, terrified; his legs give way and his knees knock together. The party is over.

f.w: the joints of his loins were loosed
f.g: His legs gave out from fear.

n: The king offers rich rewards to anyone who can read it: royal purple (scarlet), a gold chain, and the rank of third ruler. Third, because Nabonidus was first and Belshazzar second.

f.g: Purple—a color reserved for royalty and high officials.

f.w: the third ruler in the kingdom
f.g: Fits the history: Nabonidus and Belshazzar ruled first and second.

n: The wise men can’t read it or explain it.
The king’s terror grows, and his nobles are bewildered.
The queen—probably the queen mother, perhaps Nebuchadnezzar’s widow or daughter—comes in, having heard the commotion. She calmly reassures the king.

f.g: Likely the queen mother, since the king’s wives were already at the feast.

n: She remembers a man with the spirit of the holy gods, whom Nebuchadnezzar had made chief of the wise men. Daniel had apparently been forgotten by the new regime.
She praises Daniel’s gifts: he explains dreams, solves riddles, and unravels hard problems.
Daniel, now about 80 years old, is brought in. The king identifies him somewhat condescendingly as one of the exiles from Judah.
Belshazzar repeats what he has heard about Daniel’s wisdom.
He admits that his wise men failed.
He offers Daniel the same rich rewards.
Daniel politely declines the rewards—keep your gifts—but agrees to read the writing. God’s message is not for sale.

f.w: Let thy gifts be to thyself

n: Before interpreting, Daniel gives a history lesson: the Most High God gave Nebuchadnezzar his kingdom and glory.
Nebuchadnezzar’s power was absolute—he could kill or spare, promote or demote whomever he wished.
But when he became proud, God removed him from his throne and stripped his glory.
Daniel recalls Nebuchadnezzar’s humiliation among the animals until he learned that God rules over human kingdoms.

f.w: the most high God ruled in the kingdom of men

n: The heart of the charge: “You knew all this, and still did not humble yourself.” Sinning against knowledge is especially serious.
Belshazzar has defied the Lord of heaven by profaning His vessels and praising lifeless idols—while ignoring the God who holds his very breath and controls all his ways.

f.w: which see not, nor hear, nor know
the God in whose hand thy breath is

n: That is why God sent the hand and the writing.
The inscription reads: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN. These are Aramaic words for weights or coins—a mina, a shekel, and half-minas—and they also carry verbal meanings.

f.g: Units of weight/money: mina, shekel, and half-shekels (“u-” = and). Daniel reads them as verbs.

n: MENE means “numbered”: God has counted the days of your kingdom and brought it to an end.

f.g: From a root meaning “to count” or “number.”

n: TEKEL means “weighed”: you have been weighed on God’s scales and found too light—lacking in moral worth.

f.w: Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting

n: PERES (singular of PARSIN) means “divided,” and sounds like “Paras,” Persia. Your kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians.
Belshazzar keeps his word and honors Daniel—but the honor will last only a few hours.
That same night, Belshazzar is killed. Ancient historians record that the Persians took Babylon in 539 BC, some saying it happened during a festival.

f.w: In that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain

n: “Darius the Mede” takes over at about 62 years old. He is not yet identified in other ancient records; scholars suggest he may be another name for Cyrus or for a governor such as Gubaru.

f.g: Not clearly identified outside Daniel; possibly a governor under Cyrus or a title for Cyrus himself.
